before: He raised with his own hands, on the shore, the mast that Sergesthus' shattered galley had borne.
after: On the shore he raised the mast from Serestus' ship with his own hands.
reason: V.487 ingentique manu malum de nave Seresti. Serestus and the Centaur’s captain Sergestus are distinct.

before: the unconquered offspring of the Danes march behind
after: the still-unconquered Dahae march behind
reason: VIII.728 indomitique Dahae, a Central Asian people. Dryden substitutes Danes.

before: fires some of his ships (which are transformed into sea nymphs)
after: tries to burn his ships, which are transformed into sea nymphs
reason: IX.110–22 the goddess intervenes before Turnus can burn the fleet.

before: Plunged in the flood, he made the waters fly.
after: At last he leaped into the river in full armor, scattering the water.
reason: IX.815–18 restores missing subject and deliberate leap, also missing in the raw Dryden witness.

before: the two bold brothers of Sarpedon's blood, Asius and Acmon; both Assaraci; young Haemon, and, though young, resolved to die. With these were joined Clarus and Thymoetes; Tibris and Castor, both of Lycian kind.
after: Asius, son of Imbrasus, and Thymoetes, son of Hicetaon; the two men named Assaracus; the older Thymbris and Castor. With them stood Sarpedon's two brothers, and Clarus and Thaemon from the Lycian highlands.
reason: X.123–26 corrects parentage and catalogue conflations.

before: from Asium and Cosa
after: from Clusium and Cosa
reason: X.167 Clusi, Clusium, not Asium.

before: fierce tigers, reined and curbed
after: two lions, reined and curbed
reason: X.253 biiugique ad frena leones.

before: the newly raised and raw clowns
after: the newly raised, inexperienced farmers
reason: Modern sense of clowns misrepresents agrestis and historical rural sense.

before: who, not like others born, was ripped and torn from his wretched mother; sacred, O Phoebus, to you from his birth, for his beginning life was free from biting steel.
after: who had been cut from his mother after her death and dedicated to you, Phoebus. What good had it done him to escape death by steel as an infant?
reason: X.315–17 exsectum iam matre perempta; restores mother’s death and rhetorical question.

before: and sought polluted joys with obscene lust; the Trojan sword would have cured his love of boys, had not his seven bold brethren stopped the course of the fierce champion, with united force.
after: his latest love; the Trojan sword would have ended his lifelong love of young men, had not seven brothers, sons of Phorcus, stood together to block the fierce champion.
reason: X.324–29 distinguishes Phorcus’ sons from Cydon’s brothers and removes a moral condemnation added by Dryden to the Latin narrator.

before: pierced his right arm, and holding on, bereft him of the use of both, and pinioned down his left.
after: passed through his right arm and flew on, bloody, along its original course. The dying arm hung from his shoulder by its tendons.
reason: X.338–42 no left-arm pinioning, severed right arm remains attached by sinews.

before: Jove is impartial, and to both the same.
after: My father can accept either outcome.
reason: X.450 sorti pater aequus utrique est refers to Evander accepting victory or an honorable death, not Jupiter’s neutrality.

before: Eurytion's artful hands
after: the skillful hands of Clonus, son of Eurytus,
reason: X.499 Clonus Eurytides; distinct craftsman.

before: Then brave Messapus slew Ericetes, who drew his lineage from Lycaon's blood. But Ericetes found his fate from his headstrong horse, who threw his master, as he made a bound: the chief, alighting, stuck him to the ground. Then Clonius, hand to hand, on foot assails; the Trojan sinks, and Neptune's son prevails.
after: Then Messapus killed Cronius, who lay on the ground after a fall from his unruly horse, and Erichaetes, son of Lycaon, who fought on foot.
reason: X.749–52 restores names and correct association of horse fall.

before: the great Antronius
after: Thronius
reason: X.753 Thronium.

before: infernal Ate
after: pale Tisiphone
reason: X.761 pallida Tisiphone, not Ate.

before: or like a mountain ash, whose roots are spread, deep fixed in earth, while in clouds he hides his head.
after: or like Orion carrying an ancient ash tree down from the mountain peaks, walking on the earth with his head hidden among the clouds.
reason: X.766–67 Orion carries ash tree, not compared with rooted tree.

before: well-boiled oak
after: fire-hardened oak
reason: XI.553 robore cocto, hardened by heat, not boiled.

before: Astonished Aunus just arrives
after: The astonished son of Aunus just arrives
reason: XI.699–700 Appenninicolae ... filius Auni, father and son distinct.

before: through unsinged flames we march
after: we walk unsinged through the flames
reason: English misplaced modifier made the flames unsinged rather than the worshippers.

before: Then he slew Dares, Butes, and Sybaris, whom his stumbling horse had thrown over its neck.
after: With a spear he sent Asbytes to join Eumedes in death. He killed Chloreus, Sybaris, Dares, Thersilochus, and Thymoetes, whom his unruly horse had thrown over its neck.
reason: XII.362–64 restores named fighters and correct victim of horse fall.

before: Cethegus, Tanais, and Tagus
after: Cethegus, Tanais, and Talos
reason: XII.513 Talon, distinct from Tagus.

before: Nor, Cisseus, could you escape Turnus's hand, though you were the strongest of the Arcadian band.
after: Nor could your right hand save you from Turnus, Cretheus, bravest of the Greeks.
reason: XII.538 Cretheu ... Graium fortissime.

before: Iolas fell
after: Aeolus fell
reason: XII.542 Aeole; wrong personal name in Dryden.

before: In heaven they were called the Dirae, and they stood
after: Two of the sisters were called the Dirae; the third was Megaera of Tartarus. The Dirae stood
reason: XII.845–47 distinguishes pair of Dirae from their sister Megaera.

before: Ilioneus, as bold Lucetius came to force the gate, and to feed the kindling flame, rolled down the fragment of a rock so truly, that it crushed him double underneath the weight. Young Liger and Asylas slew two more: young Liger knew better how to bend the bow; Asylas best threw the pointed javelin. Brave Caeneus laid Ortygius on the plain; the victor Caeneus was slain by Turnus. By the same hand, Clonius and Itys fell, Sagar, and Ida, standing on the wall. From the arms of Capys, Privernus met his fate: hurt first by Themilla (but slight the wound), his shield thrown by, to mitigate the smart, he clapped his hand upon the wounded part; the second shaft came swift and unespied, and pierced his hand, and nailed it to his side, transfixed his breathing lungs and beating heart: the soul came issuing out, and hissed against the dart.
after: Ilioneus, as bold Lucetius came to force the gate, and to feed the kindling flame, rolled down the fragment of a rock so truly, that it crushed him double underneath the weight. Liger killed Emathion, and Asylas killed Corynaeus: Liger was skilled with the javelin, Asylas with the arrow that strikes from afar. Brave Caeneus laid Ortygius on the plain; the victor Caeneus was slain by Turnus. By the same hand, Clonius and Itys fell, Sagar, and Ida, standing on the wall. From the arms of Capys, Privernus met his fate: hurt first by Themilla (but slight the wound), his shield thrown by, to mitigate the smart, he clapped his hand upon the wounded part; the second shaft came swift and unespied, and pierced his hand, and nailed it to his side, transfixed his breathing lungs and beating heart: the soul came issuing out, and hissed against the dart.
reason: IX.571–572; Williams confirms weapon attribution.

before: Who first, and who last, heroic maid, were laid by your courage on the cold earth? Your spear of mountain ash, driven with fury, transpierced Eumenius first, from side to side: a purple stream came spouting from the wound; bathed in his blood he lies, and bites the ground. Liris and Pegasus she slew at once: the former, as he drew the slackened reins of his faint steed; the latter, as he stretched his arm to prop his friend, the javelin reached. Both fall together by the same weapon, sent from the same hand, and both spurn the sand. Amastrus next is added to the slain: she follows the rest in rout over the plain: Tereus, Harpalycus, Demophoon, and Chromis, all shun her fury at full speed. Not one of her deadly darts was lost; each was attended with a Trojan ghost. Young Ornithus bestrode a hunter steed, swift for the chase, and of Apulian breed. Him from afar she spied, in unknown arms: over his broad back an ox's hide was thrown; his helm was a wolf, whose gaping jaws were spread as a covering for his cheeks, and grinned around his head; he clenched in his hand an iron prong, and towered above the rest, conspicuous in the throng. She soon singled him out from the flying train, and slew him with ease; then she thus insults the slain: "Vain hunter, did you think to chase through woods the savage herd, a vile and trembling race? Here cease your vaunts, and own my victory: a woman warrior was too strong for you. Yet, if the ghosts demand the conqueror's name, confess it was great Camilla, to save your shame." Then Butes and Orsilochus she slew, the bulkiest bodies of the Trojan crew; but Butes breast to breast: the spear descends above the gorget, where his helmet ends, and over the shield which defends his left side. Orsilochus and she ply their courses: he seems to follow, and she seems to flee; but in a narrower ring she makes the race; and then he flees, and she pursues the chase. Gathering at length on her deluded foe, she swings her axe, and rises to the blow full on the helm behind, with such a sway the weapon falls, the riven steel gives way: he groans, he roars, he sues in vain for grace; brains, mingled with his blood, besmear his face.
after: Who first, and who last, heroic maid, were laid by your courage on the cold earth? Your long fir spear, driven with fury, first pierced the exposed chest of Eunaeus, son of Clytius: a purple stream came spouting from the wound; bathed in his blood he lies, and bites the ground. Liris and Pagasus she slew at once: the former, as he drew the reins as his stabbed horse threw him; the latter, as he stretched his arm to prop his friend, the javelin reached. Both fall together by the same weapon, sent from the same hand, and both spurn the sand. Amastrus next is added to the slain: she follows the rest in rout over the plain: Tereus, Harpalycus, Demophoon, and Chromis, all shun her fury at full speed. Not one of her deadly darts was lost; each was attended with a Trojan ghost. Young Ornithus bestrode a hunter steed, swift for the chase, and of Apulian breed. Him from afar she spied, in unknown arms: over his broad back an ox's hide was thrown; his helm was a wolf, whose gaping jaws were spread as a covering for his cheeks, and grinned around his head; he clenched in his hand an iron prong, and towered above the rest, conspicuous in the throng. She soon singled him out from the flying train, and slew him with ease; then she thus insults the slain: "Vain hunter, did you think to chase through woods the savage herd, a vile and trembling race? Here cease your vaunts, and own my victory: a woman warrior was too strong for you. Yet, if the ghosts demand the conqueror's name, confess it was great Camilla, to save your shame." Then Butes and Orsilochus she slew, the bulkiest bodies of the Trojan crew; but Butes with his back turned: the spear descends above the gorget, where his helmet ends, and over the shield which defends his left side. Orsilochus and she ply their courses: he seems to follow, and she seems to flee; but in a narrower ring she makes the race; and then he flees, and she pursues the chase. Gathering at length on her deluded foe, she swings her axe, and rises to the blow full on the helm behind, with such a sway the weapon falls, the riven steel gives way: he groans, he roars, he sues in vain for grace; brains, mingled with his blood, besmear his face.
reason: XI.666–672 and 690–693: name, spear wood, horse injury and direction of fatal blow.

before: Then Clausus came, who led a numerous band of troops embodied from the Sabine land, and, in himself alone, brought an army. It was he who begot the noble Claudian race—the Claudian race, ordained, in times to come, to share in the greatness of imperial Rome. He led forth the Cures, of old renown; the Mutuscans from their olive-bearing town; and all the Eretian powers; besides a band that followed from the dewy land of Velinum; and the Amiternian troops of mighty fame; and the mountaineers, who came from Severus, and from the craggy cliffs of Tetrica; and those where yellow Tiber takes his way, and where Himella's wanton waters play. Casperia sent her arms, with those that lie by Fabaris, and by fruitful Foruli. The warlike aids of Horta next appeared, and the cold Nursians came to close the rear, mixed with the natives born of Latin blood, whom Allia washes with her fatal flood. Not thicker billows beat the Libyan main, when pale Orion sets in wintry rain; nor thicker harvests rise on rich Hermus, or in the Lycian fields, when Phoebus burns the skies, than stood these troops: their bucklers rang around; their trampling turned the turf, and shook the solid ground.
after: Then Clausus came, who led a numerous band of troops embodied from the Sabine land, and, in himself alone, brought an army. It was he who begot the noble Claudian race—the Claudian race, ordained, in times to come, to share in the greatness of imperial Rome. He led forth the Cures, of old renown; the Mutuscans from their olive-bearing town; and all the Eretian powers; besides a band from Nomentum and the fields of Rosea by the Velinus; and the Amiternian troops of mighty fame; and the mountaineers, who came from Severus, and from the craggy cliffs of Tetrica; and those where yellow Tiber takes his way, and where Himella's wanton waters play. Casperia sent her arms, with those that lie by Fabaris, and by fruitful Foruli. The warlike aids of Horta next appeared, and the cold Nursians came to close the rear, mixed with the natives born of Latin blood, whom Allia washes with her fatal flood. Not thicker billows beat the Libyan main, when pale Orion sets in wintry rain; nor thicker harvests rise on rich Hermus, or in the Lycian fields, when Phoebus burns the skies, than stood these troops: their bucklers rang around; their trampling turned the turf, and shook the solid ground.
reason: Independent follow-up: VII.712 names Nomentum and Rosea; Rosea is a place-name, not dewy. Restores missing name and corrects mistranslation.
